The Suzuki–Miyaura coupling of aryl chlorides with arylboronic acids 
catalysed by NHC platinum complexes

Anna Smoczy´nska a, Sylwia Ostrowska a
, Anna Chojnacka a, Steven P. Nolan b,*
,  
Cezary Pietraszuk a,*

a Adam Mickiewicz University, Faculty of Chemistry, Uniwersytetu Pozna´nskiego 8, Pozna´n 61-614, Poland
b Department of Chemistry and Center for Sustainable Chemistry, Ghent University, Krijgslaan 281 (S-3), 9000 Ghent, Belgium
A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords:
N-heterocyclic carbenes
Platinum complexes
Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling
Arylboronic acids
A B S T R A C T

The platinum complexes [Pt(IPr)(DMS)Cl2] and [Pt(IPr*)(DMS)Cl2] are highly effective catalysts in the Suzu­
ki–Miyaura coupling reaction involving aryl chlorides and aryl- and alkenylboronic acids. A procedure for the 
selective synthesis of a series of biphenyls is presented. The reaction can be scaled up to at least the gram level. A 
proposed mechanism for the process is outlined.
1. Introduction

Since the landmark work of Suzuki and Miyaura [1,2], coupling of 
organic halides with organoboronic acids or their esters is commonly 
catalysed by palladium complexes [3]. However, subsequent in­
vestigations have revealed the catalytic activity of several other transi­
tion metal complexes facilitating this transformation [4]. To date, 
examples of efficient catalysis of the Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling in 
the presence of nickel [5], iron [6], cobalt [7,8] and copper [9,10] 
complexes have been described. Although aryl chlorides are the 
cheapest and most accessible aryl halides, they represent a more chal­
lenging choice of reactant for coupling due to their higher C-Cl bond 
energy compared to other C-X bonds. Currently, aryl chlorides are effi­
ciently converted by complexes of Pd [11–13], Ni [5], Co [7,8,14,15], 
and Fe [16]. NHC platinum complexes are less popular than analogous 
complexes of other platinum metals. First synthesised by Arduengo in 
1994 [17], it took a long time for them to find catalytic applications. In 
2002, Marko described a series of platinum complexes with the general 
formula [NHC-Pt(dvtms)] (dvtms = 1,3-divinyltetramethyldisiloxane), 
demonstrating their catalytic activity in the hydrosilylation of olefins 
[18]. A family of Marko catalysts was quickly developed, demonstrating 
activity in selected organic transformations [19]. Fig. 1 illustrates a 
variety of structures of NHC platinum complexes that exhibit catalytic 
activity [18,20,21].

To date, the most efficient platinum-based homogeneous systems 
have been described by Sabounchei [22] and Bedford [23], with the

latter reporting the coupling of 4-chloroacetophenone with phenyl­
boronic acid, achieving a conversion of 29 % and a TON of 58 with the 
platinacyclic complex 1a (see Fig. 2). Among heterogeneous platinum- 
based catalysts, platinum nanoparticles supported on a hierarchically 
porous polymer exhibit the highest activity. This catalyst is active in the 
coupling of chlorobenzene and a set of other chloroarenes with phe­
nylboronic acid [24]. Our interest in the catalytic activity of platinum 
NHC complexes has resulted in the development of efficient hydro­
silylation procedures for olefins and/or acetylenes [25–28] as well as the 
discovery of a highly effective and selective acetylene dimerization 
process [29].

In this article, we describe a homogeneous catalytic system based on 
NHC platinum complexes capable of efficiently performing the Suzuki- 
Miyaura cross-coupling of inactivated aryl chlorides with boronic acids.
2. Results and discussion

Exploration of the catalytic activity of N-heterocyclic carbene plat­
inum complexes of the general formula [Pt(NHC)(DMS)Cl2] (DMS =
dimethyl sulphide) recently developed by Nolan [27] (Fig. 1, 1b-e) 
revealed their excellent catalytic performance in Suzuki–Miyaura 
coupling reactions involving aryl chlorides. Adding 1 mol% of the [Pt 
(IPr)(DMS)Cl2] (1b) complex to an ethanol solution of 4-chlorotoluene 
(3a) and 4-methoxyphenylboronic acid in the presence of KOH at 80 
◦C caused the initially clear, straw-coloured solution to gradually cloud. 
After 20 h, GC/MS analysis of the light brown reaction mixture revealed

identified as 4-methoxy-4′-methyl-1,1′-biphenyl (4aa) (see Scheme 1). 
The product identity was confirmed by 1H NMR spectroscopy. The white 
precipitate formed during the reaction was filtered off and identified as 
potassium chloride.

An analogous reaction using 4-bromotoluene resulted in complete 
conversion of the aryl bromide within 15 min.

A series of experiments were performed to determine the active 
catalysts/catalytic systems and the conditions for efficient reactions. 
The catalytic activity of 1b was compared to that of 1c, 1d, and to its 
IMes analogue [Pt(IMes)(DMS)Cl2] (1e) (Table 1 entries 2–4). Further­
more, the catalytic activity of selected analogous platinum complexes, 
including the Marko type catalyst [Pt(IPr*)(dvtms)] (Table 2, entry 5) 
[30], Karstedt catalyst (Table 2, entry 6) [31] and [PtCl2(DMS)2] re­
ported by Nolan [32], was investigated. It was observed that the cata­
lytic activity strongly depends on the stereoelectronic properties of the 
NHC ligand. In the presence of complexes 1b and 1d, the reaction pro­
ceeded almost quantitatively, whereas the use of [Pt(IMes)(DMS)Cl2] 
results in no reaction (Table 1 entries 1 and 3, respectively). The high 
catalytic activity of complexes containing the IPr [33] and IPr* [34] 
ligands is well documented in palladium and other platinum metal 
catalysis. No catalytic activity was observed for both the Marko catalyst 
(1f) (see Table 1, entry 5), for the NHC ligand-free Karstedt catalyst (see 
Table 1, entry 6) and [PtCl2(DMS)2]. The reason for the lack of activity 
of the Marko catalyst may be the presence of a reluctantly dissociating 
dvtms ligand. Similarly to the case of catalysis with palladium com­
plexes, the lack of activity of complexes not containing strongly 
electron-donating and sterically extended ligands, such as NHC, results 
from an inability to carry out effective oxidative addition of the strong C- 
Cl bond to the Pt complex, as well as an inability to carry out reductive 
elimination in an uncrowded coordination sphere.

Experiments to determine the optimum base, solvent and reaction 
temperature are summarized in Table 2. The reaction does not proceed 
in the absence of platinum and under base-free conditions. The presence 
of water in reaction system has a significant effect on the course of the 
reaction. In 96 % ethanol, the reaction proceeded almost quantitative, 
while in ethanol (99.8 %), no reaction was observed (Table 2, entries 1 
and 2). Changing ethanol as a solvent to another alcohol resulted in a 
significant decrease in yield (see Table 2, entries 5 and 6). The use of 1,4- 
dioxane or toluene as a solvent, to which 10 µL of water has been added, 
results in trace amounts or no coupling product (see Table 2, entries 7 
and 8). Potassium containing bases were found more effective than the 
ones based on caesium. KOH enabled the highest performance. By 
contrast, no reaction was observed in the presence of sodium carbonate 
or hydroxide. The lower activity of sodium derivatives is probably due to 
the higher solubility of NaCl compared to KCl in ethanol, although there 
may be other reasons as well. In palladium-catalysed coupling reactions, 
sodium-containing bases also show reduced activity, a phenomenon 
most often associated with solubility issues. Other tested bases, such as 
Et3N and TBAOH, were found to be inactive. Reducing the reaction 
temperature to 60 ◦C (see Table 2, entry 18) significantly reduced the
reaction yield. No conversion was observed at room temperature.

Subsequent experiments attempted to determine the optimum cata­
lyst concentration. The results are summarized in Table 3.

All attempts to reduce the catalyst loading below 1 mol% results in a 
significant drop in reaction efficiency (see Table 3). On the other hand, 
increasing the temperature to 100 ◦C for reactions with lower catalyst 
loading resulted in a 20 % increase in reaction yield and productivity 
(see Table 3, entries 2 and 3). Under optimal conditions, a TON value of 
152 was obtained (see Table 3, Entry 3). The optimal reaction conditions 
were used to study the scope of the reaction (Scheme 2). Efficient re­
actions were obtained in the presence of aryl chlorides regardless of the 
electron properties of the substituents at the para position in the aro­
matic ring. High yields were obtained for sterically hindered 2-chloro- 
1,3-dimethylbenzene (4ad) as well as for heterocyclic derivatives. A 
lower yield of coupling product (4af, 53 %) was obtained only in the 
case of 2-chloropyridine, which is known to be a challenging reagent.

The reactivity of selected arylboronic acids with different sub­
stituents at the phenyl ring was also tested in the reaction (see Scheme 
3). The formation of the expected coupling products was observed, with 
high or satisfactory yields.

To investigate the scope of the reaction in more detail, the activity of 
styrylboronic acid (2e) was tested. When 2e reacted with 4-chloroto­
luene, the expected cross-coupling product was produced, with an 
isolation yield of 82 % (Scheme 4a). This demonstrates the activity of 
alkenylboronic acids in Suzuki cross-coupling catalysed by NHC plat­
inum complexes. In contrast, coupling the pinacol ester of phenyl­
ethynylboronic acid (2f) with p-chlorotoluene (see Scheme 4b) 
produced the desired product, albeit with an unsatisfactory isolation 
efficiency of just 22 %. The low isolation yield of 4fa was mainly due to 
the low conversion of 3a (48 %) but also due to the formation of a semi- 
hydrogenated by-product.

As products containing pyridine derivatives have high potential for 
use as building blocks in medicinal chemistry and materials science, as 
well as in coordination complexes, the scalability of the system was 
tested in the reaction of 4-methoxyphenylboronic acid with 3-chloropyr­
idine. The scale-up process enabled the synthesis of 3-(4-methox­
yphenyl)pyridine (4ae) to be carried out with an excellent yield of 95 % 
(see Scheme 5).

To gain insight into the reaction mechanism, a series of tests and 
preliminary kinetic experiments was conducted. To assess whether the 
process proceeds according to the Pt(II)/Pt(IV) cycle, reactions of [Pt 
(IPr)(DMS)Cl2] with an excess of 4-chlorotoluene were carried out at 
room temperature and at 80 ◦C. Analysis of the reaction mixtures using 
1H NMR spectroscopy showed no changes in the system. Furthermore, a 
test reaction was carried out to couple 4-methoxyphenylboronic acid 
(2a) and 4-chlorotoluene (3a) in the presence of a twofold molar excess 
of ascorbic acid relative to the catalyst [35]. This was done under the 
assumption that any active Pt(IV) complexes would be reduced during 
the coupling reaction, resulting in a significant decrease in reaction 
yield. However, the experiment did not reveal any decrease in reaction 
yield. It was therefore assumed that the reaction could proceed

In order to gain a better understanding of the reaction mechanism, 
the reaction profiles of the catalysts [Pt(IPr)(DMS)Cl2] and [Pt(IPr*) 
(DMS)Cl2] were compared (Fig. S1). Unexpectedly, the experiment 
revealed high similarity in the reaction profiles. Previous observations of 
palladium complexes indicated significantly higher catalytic activity in 
complexes containing the bulkier ligand IPr*. Interestingly, Fig. S1 
shows that the reaction rate is independent of the concentration of aryl 
chloride. Preliminary kinetic studies also showed a first-order depen­
dence of the reaction rate on the catalyst concentration and a second 
order dependence on the concentration of boronic acid (Figs. S2–S4). 
The results obtained suggest that the reaction rate (for concentrations of 
[Pt(IPr)(DMS)Cl2] = 1–2 mol%) is determined by the rate of catalyst 
initiation. The proposed catalyst initiation scheme (Scheme 6) starts 
with the reversible dissociation of DMS from [Pt(IPr)(DMS)Cl2]. This 
step was confirmed by a catalytic test, which revealed that the reaction 
is significantly suppressed in the presence of a fivefold excess of DMS 
relative to the catalyst. The next step of the initiation process is trans­
metalation, which results in the formation of a biaryl complex. Based on 
the results of catalytic studies, we propose that this process limits the 
reaction rate. The sequence of initiating the actual catalyst – the [(NHC) 
Pt(0)] complex – is completed by a process of reductive elimination. This 
step is confirmed by the observation of the of 4,4′-dimethoxy-1,1′- 
biphenyl in the reaction system. Following the generation of a

catalytically active Pt(0) complex, we propose a mechanism analogous 
to that observed for palladium complexes. This involves a sequence of 
processes comprising oxidative addition, transmetalation and reductive 
elimination. The presence of an NHC ligand is essential for the reaction 
to proceed. As with palladium complexes, strong σ-donor properties 
facilitate the oxidative addition of aryl chlorides, while bulky structures 
enable reductive elimination.

A comparison of the properties of platinum and palladium catalysts 
in the coupling reaction of aryl chlorides with arylboronic acids clearly 
shows that platinum complexes have several orders of magnitude lower 
yield and activity compared to highly active palladium-based systems 
[36]. The influence of the stereoelectronic properties of NHC ligands on 
the activity of platinum complexes appears to be similar to that observed 
for palladium complexes. The range of reactions appears to be similar 
and includes both aryl and heteroaryl derivatives. A significant advan­
tage of platinum catalysts is their total inactivity in the homocoupling of 
arylboronic acids. This prevents the formation of one of the main un­
desirable by-products. Improving the efficiency and activity of platinum 
catalysts in the activation of aryl and alkenyl chlorides is the greatest 
challenge for platinum-based coupling catalysts. This challenge can be 
met through the rational design of new platinum complexes with 
potentially higher catalytic activity and through the search for reusable 
catalysts, such as the recently described catalyst containing platinum 
nanoparticles deposited on a hierarchically porous polymer, which is

3. Conclusions

In conclusion, NHC platinum complexes [Pt(IPr)(DMS)Cl2] and [Pt 
(IPr*)(DMS)Cl2] serve as efficient precatalysts of Suzuki coupling of aryl 
chlorides and aryl- or alkenylboronic acids. The developed catalytic

system is scalable to the gram scale without significant loss of efficiency. 
A mechanism involving a Pt(0)/Pt(II) cycle has been proposed. Pre­
liminary kinetic investigations have shown that the initiation of the 
(NHC)Pt(0) complex is the rate-limiting step of the process. Ongoing 
mechanistic studies dealing with this specific issue are presently ongoing 
in our laboratories as are studies dealing with related platinum- 
mediated transformations.
4. Methods
4.1. General information

Air- and moisture-sensitive reactions were carried out under an 
argon atmosphere using standard Schlenk techniques. Solvents used for 
all experiments were purchased from Sigma Aldrich (Merck), dried over 
molecular sieves, and degassed by bubbling with argon. NHC platinum 
complexes were prepared using the methods previously described [27]. 
The (4-(ethoxycarbonyl)phenyl)boronic acid was purchased from 
Frontier Scientific, and the remaining arylboronic acids were purchased 
from FluoroChem, and used as received. All aryl chlorides were pur­
chased from Sigma Aldrich (Merck) and used as received. Potassium 
carbonate, potassium tert-butoxide, potassium phosphate, and potas­
sium hydroxide were purchased from Sigma Aldrich (Merck), dried 
under high vacuum, and stored protected from moisture and air. EtOH 
(96 %) was purchased from POCh (Poland). The progress of the re­
actions was monitored by gas chromatography (GC), using dodecane as 
an internal standard. GC analyses were performed using Varian CP-3800 
(column: RTX-5 30 m ID 0.53 mm), equipped with TCD. GC/MS analyses 
were performed on an Agilent 5977B GC/MSD with an Agilent 8860 GC 
System. The structures of the complexes and hydrogenation products 
were determined by NMR spectroscopy and elemental analysis. 1H NMR 
(600 MHz) and 13C NMR (100 and 151 MHz) spectra were recorded on 
an Avance I (Bruker) spectrometer at 600 MHz using chloroform‑d1 
(CDCl3) as the solvent.
